title: A Classroom Investigation
paragraphs: A class was investigating how writers turn observations into evidence. The teacher supplied a folder of short accounts and asked the students to look beyond their first impressions. Each account described a particular situation, but the collection raised questions that could apply more widely.
Several records provided a starting point for the discussion. Without a map, tourists may wander through the streets for hours.

By the end of the discussion, the students had learned why careful reading requires more than a quick judgment. A useful interpretation must fit the details of the situation. They chose a conclusion that acknowledged differences among the accounts, and they left readers with a question: which observation most strongly supports your view, and what might change your mind?

A reader can continue the investigation by choosing one detail and explaining why it matters. The strongest answer will distinguish observation from assumption, consider the circumstances, and identify a question that would require more evidence before it could be answered confidently.
